- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. # Cerne — Requirements and Screen Flow

Cerne is a reflective-journaling mobile app with an AI assistant. The user records their day by text, audio or photo; a conversational agent consults those records (semantic search) to answer with context and to offer insights.

This document is the product specification. The visual reference is the prototype in `docs/input/prototype/`; the backend API is documented in `docs/input/backend/`.

---

## 1. Functional requirements

### RF01 — Multimodal capture (text / audio / photo)
Data entry by text, real-time audio recording and photo upload — always through Screen 2 (Insertion Modal), which has a raw text field in addition to the microphone and the gallery. Every capture becomes a persisted record (`POST /entries`), **distinct from a chat message** (see the separation note in RF04).

**Acceptance criteria:**
- The three modalities (text, audio, photo) result in the same persisted-entry format — none is treated structurally differently from the others after capture.
- Cancelling a capture midway (e.g., interrupting a recording) does not create a partial or empty entry.

### RF02 — Speech-to-text / OCR processing
Transcription of audio (speech-to-text) and recognition of text in images (OCR) over the content captured in RF01.

**Acceptance criteria:** four visible states — recording, processing, transcribed, transcription error.

### RF03 — Biometric authentication vault
Access barrier via Face ID / Touch ID / PIN before exposing the user's data.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- A biometric failure (e.g., fingerprint not recognized) offers PIN as an alternative, without locking the user out of the app.
- The app, sent to the background and resumed after 5 minutes, requires authentication again — it does not stay unlocked indefinitely (fixed value, not configurable by the user).

### RF04 — Interactive chat with memory (RAG)
Continuous conversation with the AI agent, with semantic search over previous entries. **Chat messages are conversational and do not create journal entries automatically** — the only exception is the explicit save action described in RF10. Otherwise, the chat queries existing entries via RAG but does not write to them.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- Three mandatory UI states: processing/streaming, error, complete response.
- If the response stream drops midway, the partial message stays visible with a failure indication (it does not disappear).

### RF05 — Personal summary export
Generation of a narrative summary by AI (Claude Haiku 4.5) from the user's entries, exportable as PDF, with an additional option to download the raw data without the narrative. No clinical or diagnostic connotation. **Scope: job generation, file download and failure handling — never the quality of the generated narrative text.**

**Acceptance criteria:**
- An export job with zero entries in the period returns a handled error state (not an empty PDF, not a crash).
- A failure generating the narrative text (model timeout) still allows downloading the raw data without the narrative — the export is not blocked by an AI failure.

### RF06 — Semantic search / filter over journal entries
Semantic similarity search (via Voyage AI embeddings, reusing the ones already generated in RF01) combined with metadata filters (date, entry type). There is no filter by tag or category: the backend does not implement it in any endpoint — `GET /entries` and `GET /entries/search` accept only `source` and `dateFrom`/`dateTo`. Tags appear only embedded, read-only, in the `Entry` object (see section 2).

**Acceptance criteria:**
- Searching for a term finds semantically related entries even without the exact word (e.g., searching "ansiedade" returns an entry that only mentions "nervosismo", without the literal term).
- 300 ms search debounce: fast typing triggers a single query, not one per keystroke.
- Results from the local read cache stay consistent with the server after reconnection, without duplicating displayed items *(the architecture is cloud-only; offline allows only viewing already-cached data, not writing)*.
- Two or more filters applied at the same time (`source` + `dateFrom`/`dateTo`) narrow results with AND logic (not OR).
- Clearing the filters returns to the full list without restarting the screen.

### RF07 — Multi-source history (timeline)
A screen whose state depends simultaneously on authentication, synchronization status and entry data.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- Session expiration while viewing triggers a new-login prompt without a crash and without losing the scroll position.
- The per-entry synchronization status badge updates independently of the authentication stream.
- No BLoC imports another BLoC directly.

### RF08 — Proactive insights (mechanism)
A suggestion inserted into the chat without the user asking for it. **Scope: only the trigger mechanism, never the quality of the generated text.**

**Acceptance criteria:**
- Trigger after N = 5 user messages OR T = 2 min of inactivity — fires exactly once per satisfied condition.
- If insight generation fails (timeout / network error), the main chat keeps working normally.
- Dismissing the insight does not change the scroll position or the state of the main conversation.

### RF09 — Temporal summaries / dashboard
An evolution chart with a textual summary, computed on demand when the Settings tab is opened. **Scope: aggregation and rendering, never the quality of the narrative text.**

**Acceptance criteria:**
- Renders correctly in three scenarios: zero entries, one entry, more than 30 entries.
- The aggregation recalculates correctly after an entry is created (cache-invalidation test). Entries are immutable: there is no `PATCH /entries/:id` or `DELETE /entries/:id` in the backend, and no screen describes an edit or delete action on an entry.
- The AI narrative text is checked only for not breaking the UI in extreme cases — never for its content.

### RF10 — Save a chat message as an entry
A button on each user message in the chat that converts it into a persisted entry — for moments when the user states relevant information during the conversation, not only through dedicated capture (RF01). It reuses the same `POST /entries` pipeline (PII check + embedding), with the origin marked as `chat`.

Bem-vindo, Wagnerduarte. Antes de começar, uma pergunta rápida pra calibrar o desafio: este PRFAQ é sobre o **Cerne** como produto como um todo (a tese de que um app de journaling reflexivo com assistente de IA resolve um problema real o suficiente para existir), ou sobre uma fatia específica dele — por exemplo os insights proativos (RF08) ou o resumo narrativo (RF05), que são as partes mais "vendíveis" e mais fáceis de embromar?

Isso importa porque o PRFAQ força você a escrever o press release do produto *terminado* antes de construir — e, pelo que vi nos requisitos, o Cerne tem um claro risco de ficar "feature completa, tese vazia": captura multimodal, RAG, insights, resumos, exportação — tudo construído, mas falta a frase de uma linha que explica por que alguém trocaria o diário de papel (ou o Notion, ou simplesmente não escrever nada) por isto.

Antes de seguir, preciso saber:

1. **Cliente**: quem é essa pessoa, especificamente? "Quem já faz journaling e quer mais insight" é vago — pense em alguém real: idade, hábito atual, o que te fez pensar nela.
2. **Problema**: o que ela sente *hoje*, sem o Cerne? Não "falta de autoconhecimento" — isso é abstrato. O que ela faz, tenta, e onde isso falha?
3. **Stakes**: por que isso importa pra ela o suficiente pra abrir um app todo dia?
4. **Conceito de solução**: já tem o quê — o Cerne como está especificado nos requisitos, ou uma versão reduzida/reposicionada pra esse PRFAQ?

E uma última coisa de contexto: isto é um TCC (projeto acadêmico), certo? Isso muda a calibração — não existe "primeiros 100 clientes" ou "unit economics" reais aqui, então vou tratar como `concept_type` acadêmico/portfolio, a menos que você me diga que há uma ambição comercial genuína por trás.

1	# Artifact Analyzer
2	
3	You are a research analyst. Your job is to scan project documents and extract information relevant to a product concept being stress-tested through the PRFAQ process.
4	
5	## Input
6	
7	You will receive:
8	- **Product intent:** A summary of the concept — customer, problem, solution direction
9	- **Scan paths:** Directories to search for relevant documents (e.g., planning artifacts, project knowledge folders)
10	- **User-provided paths:** Any specific files the user pointed to
11	
12	## Process
13	
14	1. **Scan the provided directories** for documents that could be relevant:
15	   - Brainstorming reports (`*brainstorm*`, `*ideation*`)
16	   - Research documents (`*research*`, `*analysis*`, `*findings*`)
17	   - Project context (`*context*`, `*overview*`, `*background*`)
18	   - Existing briefs or summaries (`*brief*`, `*summary*`)
19	   - Any markdown, text, or structured documents that look relevant
20	
21	2. **For sharded documents** (a folder with `index.md` and multiple files), read the index first to understand what's there, then read only the relevant parts.
22	
23	3. **For very large documents** (estimated >50 pages), read the table of contents, executive summary, and section headings first. Read only sections directly relevant to the stated product intent. Note which sections were skimmed vs read fully.
24	
25	4. **Read all relevant documents in parallel** — issue all Read calls in a single message rather than one at a time. Extract:
26	   - Key insights that relate to the product intent
27	   - Market or competitive information
28	   - User research or persona information

# Artifact Analyzer

You are a research analyst. Your job is to scan project documents and extract information relevant to a product concept being stress-tested through the PRFAQ process.

## Input

You will receive:
- **Product intent:** A summary of the concept — customer, problem, solution direction
- **Scan paths:** Directories to search for relevant documents (e.g., planning artifacts, project knowledge folders)
- **User-provided paths:** Any specific files the user pointed to

## Process

1. **Scan the provided directories** for documents that could be relevant:
   - Brainstorming reports (`*brainstorm*`, `*ideation*`)
   - Research documents (`*research*`, `*analysis*`, `*findings*`)
   - Project context (`*context*`, `*overview*`, `*background*`)
   - Existing briefs or summaries (`*brief*`, `*summary*`)
   - Any markdown, text, or structured documents that look relevant

2. **For sharded documents** (a folder with `index.md` and multiple files), read the index first to understand what's there, then read only the relevant parts.

3. **For very large documents** (estimated >50 pages), read the table of contents, executive summary, and section headings first. Read only sections directly relevant to the stated product intent. Note which sections were skimmed vs read fully.

4. **Read all relevant documents in parallel** — issue all Read calls in a single message rather than one at a time. Extract:
   - Key insights that relate to the product intent
   - Market or competitive information
   - User research or persona information
   - Technical context or constraints
   - Ideas, both accepted and rejected (rejected ideas are valuable — they prevent re-proposing)
   - Any metrics, data points, or evidence

5. **Ignore documents that aren't relevant** to the stated product intent. Don't waste tokens on unrelated content.

## Output

Return ONLY the following JSON object. No preamble, no commentary. Keep total response under 1,500 tokens. Maximum 5 bullets per section — prioritize the most impactful findings.

```json
{
  "documents_found": [

  ],
  "key_insights": [

  ],
  "raw_detail_worth_preserving": [
    "bullet — specific details, data points, quotes for the distillate"
  ]
}
```

# Cerne Turns Your Journal Into an AI That Remembers What You Told It

## For people who gave up on journaling because nothing ever answered back, Cerne is an AI you talk to that actually remembers your own entries — and never sends your voice off your phone

**SÃO PAULO, Brazil — March 2027** — Today marks the launch of Cerne, a mobile journaling app for people who want to think out loud about their day — by typing, speaking, or snapping a photo — and get an AI companion that remembers what they said last week, last month, or three months ago. Unlike generic AI chatbots that forget everything the moment a conversation ends, Cerne searches back through a person's own past entries to answer with real context, not generic advice.

Most people who try journaling quit within weeks. Paper notebooks pile up unread. Notes apps become a graveyard of unsearched text. A growing number of people have started typing their day out to a general-purpose AI chatbot instead — only to find every conversation starts from zero: the bot has no memory of the stressful week they mentioned a month ago, no way to connect today's frustration to a pattern from three months back. And anyone who has poured private thoughts into an AI has had the same quiet worry: who else can read this, and where does it go?

Cerne changes what it feels like to look back at your own life. Every entry — typed, spoken, or photographed — becomes something you can actually ask about later: "What was going on with me in July?" or "Have I felt this way before?" get answered with your own words, not a canned response. Voice entries are transcribed on the phone itself and never leave the device as audio. And because Cerne is explicitly not a therapy or diagnosis tool, it never pretends to analyze your mental health — it just helps you see your own patterns, in your own words, for yourself.

> "We didn't want to build another chatbot that forgets you the second you close the app. We wanted something that treats your own past the way a good friend does — remembering, without ever making you feel watched."
> — Wagner Duarte, Creator of Cerne

### How It Works

Open Cerne and the first thing you see is a simple prompt: type, talk, or snap a photo of something from your day. No setup, no mood sliders, no forced categories. A few weeks in, start a conversation — ask Cerne anything about what you've written, and it searches your own entries to answer, quoting back what you actually said instead of guessing. Every so often, without being asked, Cerne notices something — a pattern across a handful of entries, a quiet period, a recurring theme — and raises it gently inside the conversation, never as an interruption you can't dismiss. When a conversation surfaces something worth keeping, one tap saves it as its own entry, so nothing important gets lost in chat history.

> "I used to just talk to ChatGPT about my day and then... nothing. It forgot everything by the next morning. Last week I asked Cerne why I'd been so anxious lately, and it reminded me of three entries from a month ago I'd completely forgotten I wrote. That's the first time an app actually felt like it knew me."
> — early user, translated from Portuguese

### Getting Started

Cerne launches on iOS first. Behind a Face ID, Touch ID, or PIN lock from the very first screen, signing up takes under a minute — and the only setup required is your first entry, in whichever form feels easiest: typed, spoken, or photographed.

# Cerne Turns Your Journal Into an AI That Remembers What You Told It

## For people who gave up on journaling because nothing ever answered back, Cerne is an AI you talk to that actually remembers your own entries — and never sends your voice off your phone

**SÃO PAULO, Brazil — March 2027** — Today marks the launch of Cerne, a mobile journaling app for people who want to think out loud about their day — by typing, speaking, or snapping a photo — and get an AI companion that remembers what they said last week, last month, or three months ago. Unlike generic AI chatbots that forget everything the moment a conversation ends, Cerne searches back through a person's own past entries to answer with real context, not generic advice.

Most people who try journaling quit within weeks. Paper notebooks pile up unread. Notes apps become a graveyard of unsearched text. A growing number of people have started typing their day out to a general-purpose AI chatbot instead — only to find every conversation starts from zero: the bot has no memory of the stressful week they mentioned a month ago, no way to connect today's frustration to a pattern from three months back. And anyone who has poured private thoughts into an AI has had the same quiet worry: who else can read this, and where does it go?

Cerne changes what it feels like to look back at your own life. Every entry — typed, spoken, or photographed — becomes something you can actually ask about later: "What was going on with me in July?" or "Have I felt this way before?" get answered with your own words, not a canned response. Voice entries are transcribed on the phone itself and never leave the device as audio. And because Cerne is explicitly not a therapy or diagnosis tool, it never pretends to analyze your mental health — it just helps you see your own patterns, in your own words, for yourself.

> "We didn't want to build another chatbot that forgets you the second you close the app. We wanted something that treats your own past the way a good friend does — remembering, without ever making you feel watched."
> — Wagner Duarte, Creator of Cerne

### How It Works

Open Cerne and the first thing you see is a simple prompt: type, talk, or snap a photo of something from your day. No setup, no mood sliders, no forced categories. A few weeks in, start a conversation — ask Cerne anything about what you've written, and it searches your own entries to answer, quoting back what you actually said instead of guessing. Every so often, without being asked, Cerne notices something — a pattern across a handful of entries, a quiet period, a recurring theme — and raises it gently inside the conversation, never as an interruption you can't dismiss. When a conversation surfaces something worth keeping, one tap saves it as its own entry, so nothing important gets lost in chat history.

> "I used to just talk to ChatGPT about my day and then... nothing. It forgot everything by the next morning. Last week I asked Cerne why I'd been so anxious lately, and it reminded me of three entries from a month ago I'd completely forgotten I wrote. That's the first time an app actually felt like it knew me."
> — early user, translated from Portuguese

### Getting Started

Cerne launches on iOS first. Behind a Face ID, Touch ID, or PIN lock from the very first screen, signing up takes under a minute — and the only setup required is your first entry, in whichever form feels easiest: typed, spoken, or photographed.

Working Backwards cannot start from a feature list, so a persona and problem had to be reconstructed from indirect signals (UI language, architectural choices, explicit non-goals) rather than stated directly anywhere in the input package.

**Why this direction over alternatives:** Considered running the PRFAQ at the whole-app level vs. a single feature (RF08 proactive insights, or RF05 summary export) in isolation. Chose the whole-app level because the reconstructed customer problem (AI that forgets / generic AI loops / privacy anxiety about an AI reading private writing) is the thesis the entire feature set serves — RF01/RF02 (capture), RF04 (RAG chat), RF08 (proactive insight), RF05/RF09 (summary/dashboard) are all expressions of one underlying promise ("an AI that actually remembers and connects your own entries, privately"), not independent value props. # Stage 3: Customer FAQ

**Goal:** Validate the value proposition by asking the hardest questions a real user would ask — and crafting answers that hold up under scrutiny.

## The Devil's Advocate

You are now the customer. Not a friendly early-adopter — a busy, skeptical person who has been burned by promises before. You've read the press release. Now you have questions.

**Generate 6-10 customer FAQ questions** that cover these angles:

- **Skepticism:** "How is this different from [existing solution]?" / "Why should I switch from what I use today?"
- **Trust:** "What happens to my data?" / "What if this shuts down?" / "Who's behind this?"
- **Practical concerns:** "How much does it cost?" / "How long does it take to get started?" / "Does it work with [thing I already use]?"
- **Edge cases:** "What if I need to [uncommon but real scenario]?" / "Does it work for [adjacent use case]?"
- **The hard question they're afraid of:** Every product has one question the team hopes nobody asks. Find it and ask it.

**Don't generate softball questions.** "How do I sign up?" is not a FAQ — it's a CTA. Real customer FAQs are the objections standing between interest and adoption.

**Calibrate to concept type.** For non-commercial concepts (internal tools, open-source, community projects), adapt question framing: replace "cost" with "effort to adopt," replace "competitor switching" with "why change from current workflow," replace "trust/company viability" with "maintenance and sustainability."

## Coaching the Answers

Present the questions and work through answers with the user:

1. **Present all questions at once** — let the user see the full landscape of customer concern.
2. **Work through answers together.** The user drafts (or you draft and they react). For each answer:
   - Is it honest? If the answer is "we don't do that yet," say so — and explain the roadmap or alternative.
   - Is it specific? "We have enterprise-grade security" is not an answer. What certifications? What encryption? What SLA?
   - Would a customer believe it? Marketing language in FAQ answers destroys credibility.
3. **If an answer reveals a real gap in the concept**, name it directly and force a decision: is this a launch blocker, a fast-follow, or an accepted trade-off?
4. **The user can add their own questions too.** Often they know the scary questions better than anyone.

Generate questions and best-effort answers from available context. Flag answers with low confidence so a human can review.

## Customer FAQ

### Q: Is Cerne a mental health app? Can it tell if I'm struggling, or help if I am?

A: No. Cerne is explicitly not a therapy, diagnostic, or crisis tool. As of this build, there's no mechanism that detects risk signals like self-harm or suicidal ideation in what you write — that's a deliberate scope decision, not an oversight. If you're in crisis, Cerne doesn't recognize that and won't point you anywhere for help. Treat it as a tool for noticing your own patterns, not as support for a crisis.

### Q: Can anyone — including whoever built Cerne — read what I write?

A: Your entries are stored in a cloud backend, not only on your phone — Cerne has no offline-write mode. Row-level security restricts each account to its own data, the AI pipeline that processes a request doesn't retain anything beyond that request, and you can permanently and completely erase your account at any time. The one thing that genuinely never leaves your device is raw audio: voice entries are transcribed on-device, and only the resulting text — not the recording — is ever sent anywhere. That's a real privacy boundary, but it's not the same as "nothing ever leaves your phone," and you should know that distinction before trusting it with anything you'd want to stay unrecoverable.

### Q: How do I know the AI's insights and summaries are actually good, and not generic filler?

A: Honestly, this build doesn't prove that yet. What's verified is that insight and summary generation don't crash, handle failures gracefully, and render correctly — not whether the text itself is perceptive. Whether Cerne's AI responses feel genuinely specific to you, rather than the same "generic AI response" complaint leveled at every competitor in this space, is the single biggest unproven assumption behind the whole idea.

### Q: How is this different from just talking to ChatGPT about my day?

A: ChatGPT doesn't remember your past sessions — every conversation starts from zero. Cerne's chat runs a real semantic search over your own past entries before it answers, so it can reference something you wrote two months ago by meaning, not exact wording. That persistent, personal memory is the entire bet Cerne is making.

### Q: Can I edit or delete a single entry after I've written it?

A: No — entries are immutable once saved; there's no way to edit or delete just one. You can delete your entire account and everything in it, but not a single entry in isolation. If you write something you regret, today the only fix is all-or-nothing.

### Q: Does Cerne work without an internet connection?

A: You can view entries you've already loaded while offline, but you can't capture a new one — text, voice, or photo — until you're back online. Cerne doesn't queue offline writes to sync later; it simply can't create entries offline.

### Q: Can Cerne automatically organize my entries by mood or topic?

A: No — tags are manual, added by you. Automatic categorization was considered and cut from this build to keep scope realistic; it isn't in the current product.

### Q: What does Cerne cost, and will it still exist next year?

A: Cerne was built as an academic capstone project, not a commercial product — there's no pricing model, and no commitment about it being available or maintained beyond the project. If you're sizing this up as a real product rather than a student build, that's an honest open question, not a settled answer.

### Q: If I lose my phone, do I lose my journal?

A: No — your entries live in the cloud, so logging in on a new device restores your full journal. The only loss would be anything mid-capture — a recording in progress, for instance — that never finished syncing before the phone was lost.

# Stage 4: Internal FAQ

**Goal:** Stress-test the concept from the builder's side. The customer FAQ asked "should I use this?" The internal FAQ asks "can we actually pull this off — and should we?"

## The Skeptical Stakeholder

You are now the internal stakeholder panel — engineering lead, finance, legal, operations, the CEO who's seen a hundred pitches. The press release was inspiring. Now prove it's real.

**Generate 6-10 internal FAQ questions** that cover these angles:

- **Feasibility:** "What's the hardest technical problem here?" / "What do we not know how to build yet?" / "What are the key dependencies and risks?"
- **Business viability:** "What does the unit economics look like?" / "How do we acquire the first 100 customers?" / "What's the competitive moat — and how durable is it?"
- **Resource reality:** "What does the team need to look like?" / "What's the realistic timeline to a usable product?" / "What do we have to say no to in order to do this?"
- **Risk:** "What kills this?" / "What's the worst-case scenario if we ship and it doesn't work?" / "What regulatory or legal exposure exists?"
- **Strategic fit:** "Why us? Why now?" / "What does this cannibalize?" / "If this succeeds, what does the company look like in 3 years?"
- **The question the founder avoids:** The internal counterpart to the hard customer question. The thing that keeps them up at night but hasn't been said out loud.

**Calibrate questions to context.** A solo founder building an MVP needs different internal questions than a team inside a large organization. Don't ask about "board alignment" for a weekend project. Don't ask about "weekend viability" for an enterprise product. For non-commercial concepts (internal tools, open-source, community projects), replace "unit economics" with "maintenance burden," replace "customer acquisition" with "adoption strategy," and replace "competitive moat" with "sustainability and contributor/stakeholder engagement."

## Coaching the Answers

Same approach as Customer FAQ — draft, challenge, refine:

1. **Present all questions at once.**
2. **Work through answers.** Demand specificity. "We'll figure it out" is not an answer. Neither is "we'll hire for that." What's the actual plan?
3. **Honest unknowns are fine — unexamined unknowns are not.** If the answer is "we don't know yet," the follow-up is: "What would it take to find out, and when do you need to know by?"
4. **Watch for hand-waving on resources and timeline.** These are the most commonly over-optimistic answers. Push for concrete scoping.

## Headless Mode

Generate questions calibrated to context and best-effort answers. Flag high-risk areas and unknowns prominently.

## Updating the Document

Append the Internal FAQ section to the output document. Update frontmatter: `status: "internal-faq"`, `stage: 4`, `updated` timestamp.

## Coaching Notes Capture

Before moving on, append a `<!-- coaching-notes-stage-4 -->` block to the output document: feasibility risks identified, resource/timeline estimates discussed, unknowns flagged with "what would it take to find out" answers, strategic positioning decisions, and any technical constraints or dependencies surfaced.

## Stage Complete

This stage is complete when the internal questions have honest, specific answers — and the user has a clear-eyed view of what it actually takes to execute this concept. Optimism is fine. Delusion is not.

Route to `./verdict.md`.

input.new_string:
## Internal FAQ

### Q: If a committee member asks why an unverified-quality AI is the product's core differentiator, what do we say?

A: We can't claim the AI insights are actually good — only that the mechanism around them (triggering, rendering, failure handling) works. The honest defense-day answer is that this project's scope is the software-engineering challenge — Clean Architecture, state management across layers, Flutter/BLoC discipline, graceful failure handling — not prompt engineering or AI output quality, which is treated as a black box the system must handle gracefully regardless of what comes back. That's a legitimate framing for an engineering capstone, but it only holds if the written defense says this explicitly, instead of letting press-release language like "an AI that gets you" imply more than the grading actually verifies.

### Q: The planning artifacts already disagree on local caching — drift (SQLite) vs. Hive. Which is it, and does it matter?

A: Right now it isn't settled. The Flutter package research recommended `drift` for the local cache; the later forge decision overrode it to `Hive`, reasoning that since all filtering/pagination happens via server-side query params, there's no need for a relational query engine on-device. That's a defensible reason, but two of this project's own planning artifacts currently disagree and nobody has gone back to reconcile them. What it would take to resolve: explicitly marking the `drift` recommendation as superseded in the research artifact before F000 implementation starts — a five-minute fix, but only if it's done before, not after, code gets written against one assumption or the other.

### Q: What's the single hardest technical problem in this build?

A: Two candidates, both state-management problems rather than AI problems. RF07's history screen depends on three independently-changing streams at once — auth session, sync-badge status, entry data — while explicitly forbidding one BLoC from importing another. RF08's proactive-insight trigger must fire exactly once per satisfied condition (5 user messages OR 2 minutes of inactivity) without double-firing or missing the window during an active chat session. Both are solvable with standard Flutter patterns (stream combination, debounce timers), but "solvable in principle" and "built and tested" are different claims — neither exists yet.

### Q: What's the realistic timeline, and does the delivery order actually fit?

A: The input package gives a delivery order — F000 → RF03 → RF01 → RF02 → RF07 → RF06 → RF04 → RF10 → RF08 → RF05 → RF09 — but no explicit deadline date, hours-per-week budget, or buffer appears anywhere in `docs/input/` or `_bmad-output/`. That's a real unknown, not a solved one. What it would take to find out: the actual course calendar and defense date, which only the student has — until that's pinned down, nobody can say with confidence whether 10 functional requirements plus RNF07's 80%-domain-coverage bar and RNF09's 15 tested failure scenarios fit in the time available.

### Q: What kills this project — not the app, the grade?

A: Two concrete ways. First, scope creep into the explicitly excluded extension features (dynamic AI categorization, autonomous goal extraction, dynamic persona adjustment) under the pressure to make the demo look more impressive — `requirements.md` already forbids this, so the discipline has to hold under deadline stress, not just on paper. Second, a blocking bug in the frozen backend that has no code-side remedy, since "never change the backend" is a hard policy — any such bug can only be worked around or documented as a known limitation, never fixed.

### Q: What's already been said no to, and will that discipline hold?

A: The three extension features were already cut to static or manual stand-ins — manual tags instead of AI categorization, a static kanban instead of autonomous goal extraction, a cosmetic toggle instead of dynamic persona adjustment. That "no" is already on record. The open question is whether it holds when a committee member asks "why doesn't it do X" — the honest answer has to be "that was deliberately out of scope," not "we ran out of time," and those two answers land very differently in a defense.

### Q: What's the actual legal/regulatory exposure here?

A: For a real commercial launch, handling personal journal entries through a cloud backend would draw genuine LGPD scrutiny. For this project specifically, the exposure is close to zero in practice — there's no live user base beyond test/demo accounts. But the architecture still has to demonstrate the compliance posture (row-level security, hard delete, no retention in the AI pipeline) because that's part of what's being graded as sound engineering, not because real regulatory risk exists yet. Don't let "it's just a student project" become an excuse to skip demonstrating it.

### Q: What happens to Cerne after the defense?

A: No plan exists anywhere in the input package — no stated intent to publish it, maintain it, or carry it forward as a portfolio piece beyond the TCC itself. That's fine for a capstone, but worth deciding explicitly rather than leaving implicit: is this a one-time academic artifact, or is surviving this PRFAQ process also meant to produce something that works in a job-application portfolio? The answer changes how much the distribution and "Getting Started" questions from the Customer FAQ actually matter going forward.

## The Verdict

**Concept strength:** Sharp as a disciplined engineering capstone wrapped in a genuinely researched product thesis — soft wherever it depends on something outside this project's control (a deadline, a committee's reading of the scope boundary, a backend it cannot touch). The product thinking survived the gauntlet; what's underdeveloped is the plan for saying the hard parts out loud before someone else finds them.

**Forged in steel:**
- The core differentiator — persistent, semantic memory over your own entries, versus the "generic AI response" fatigue that's the #1 complaint against every competitor studied (Reflectly, Day One AI, Mindsera) and versus session-less tools like ChatGPT — is specific, researched, and survived every FAQ question aimed at it without resorting to marketing language.
- The privacy architecture is real and precisely qualified, not oversold: on-device Whisper transcription, row-level security, hard delete for LGPD are named exactly, and the Customer FAQ explicitly corrects the tempting overclaim ("nothing ever leaves your phone") to what's actually true (the audio stays local; the transcribed text does not).
- The non-clinical positioning, forced by the product's own scope decision, lines up with where the regulatory and reputational winds are actually blowing for companion/emotional-support AI right now — a genuine, evidence-backed timing advantage, not just a constraint dressed up as a feature.
- Resource discipline is already demonstrated, not promised: three extension features were concretely cut to static/manual stand-ins, on record in `requirements.md` section 2, which gives a clean, honest answer to "why doesn't it do X" instead of "we ran out of time."

**Needs more heat:**
- No deadline, hours-per-week budget, or buffer exists anywhere in the input package — feasibility of the delivery order (F000 → RF03 → … → RF09) against RNF07/RNF09's testing bars can't be honestly assessed until that date is pinned down.
- The post-defense fate of the project (one-time academic artifact vs. a piece meant to survive into a portfolio) is undecided, and it changes how much the distribution/"Getting Started" questions actually matter.
- Two cheap, already-identified fixes are sitting un-actioned: reconciling the `drift`-vs-`Hive` contradiction between two prior planning artifacts, and adding a no-detection-required crisis-resources disclaimer as a low-cost fast-follow to the non-clinical scope.

**Cracks in the foundation:**
- The deepest crack isn't in the product thinking — it's in what the written defense says about it. The press release promises an AI that "actually remembers and gets you"; the grading scope explicitly never verifies whether the generated insight is actually good, only that the mechanism around it doesn't break. That gap is a legitimate and defensible engineering-scope boundary — but only if the defense states it explicitly. Left unstated, it's exactly the unexamined assumption a committee member probing "why is an unverified AI your core differentiator" would expose as having never been confronted — when in fact this document confronted it directly. The fix is one explicit paragraph in the written defense, not a code change.
- Entry immutability (no per-entry edit/delete, forced by the frozen backend contract) is a real adoption-friction crack for any future use of this product beyond the TCC. It can't be fixed within this project's constraints, but it should be named as a known limitation on the record — not something a future reviewer or user discovers on their own.

## Concept type
Academic capstone (TCC) built and evaluated with commercial-product customer-first discipline — no unit economics or customer-acquisition targets apply; the calibration used was feasibility, delivery-order fit, and scope-discipline-under-deadline-pressure instead.

## Customer & problem (reconstructed — not stated anywhere in docs/input/)
- `docs/input/requirements.md` never names a customer or persona; it's organized entirely around RF01–RF10/screens. The persona below is a reconstruction from UI language (Portuguese), architectural choices, and explicit non-goals — flag this to any downstream PRD author as inferred, not sourced.
- Persona: a Brazilian Portuguese-speaking person who has already tried journaling (paper, Notes, Day One) and quit, or who uses a general-purpose chatbot (ChatGPT) to process their day and is frustrated it forgets everything between sessions.
- Problem: wants an AI that genuinely recalls and connects their own past entries (not generic "how did that make you feel" loops), without fear their private writing is mined, sold, or mistaken for a mental-health signal.
- Stakes: alternative today is journaling into a void that never responds, or using a memoryless, privacy-ambiguous general AI tool.

## Core differentiator (validated against real 2025-2026 competitive research)
- "Generic AI response" fatigue is the #1 complaint across AI-journaling competitors (Reflectly, Day One AI, Mindsera) — Cerne's RAG-over-own-entries is positioned directly against this, not against feature count.
- Digital journal app market: $5.69B (2025) → $6.34B (2026), ~11.4% CAGR, projected $9.64B by 2030 — healthy, growing category; mobile is >60% of usage, validating the Flutter mobile-first bet.
- Real competitors with gaps worth knowing: Mindsera (feature-sprawl, gimmicky), Rosebud (therapist-designed framing risks implying clinical utility), Reflectly (mood-tracking-shallow, blurs into mental-health claims), Day One/Journey/Stoic (AI bolted on as paywalled add-on, not core).
- Regulatory climate rewards strict non-clinical positioning: Italy fined Replika's maker (Luka) €5M; California's 2026 law mandates companion-chatbot disclosure. Cerne's explicit non-clinical scope is a timing advantage, not just a constraint.

## Honest, unresolved tension (the single most important thing for downstream PRD/architecture work to carry forward)
RF05, RF08, RF09 each explicitly scope grading to "mechanism only, never the quality of the generated narrative text" — meaning the dimension that actually determines whether a real user would stay (is the AI's insight good, or generic/canned) is never verified by this project's own acceptance criteria. This is a legitimate engineering-scope boundary, but it must be stated explicitly in any written defense/documentation — left implicit, it reads as an unexamined gap rather than a deliberate one.

## Scope signals — in, out, and why
- IN (core, already specified): multimodal capture (RF01), STT/OCR (RF02), biometric vault (RF03), RAG chat (RF04), semantic search/filter (RF06), timeline history (RF07), save-chat-as-entry (RF10), proactive insight trigger mechanism only (RF08), AI summary export mechanism only (RF05), temporal dashboard (RF09).
- OUT (explicit extension features, never implement per AGENTS.md policy): dynamic AI categorization of entries (reduced to manual tags), autonomous AI goal extraction (reduced to static kanban with example cards), dynamic AI persona adjustment (reduced to a cosmetic settings toggle). These were deliberately cut for a solo/timeline-bound build, not because they lacked value — worth remembering if scope ever gets re-opened.
- OUT (hard non-goal, stated policy): any risk-signal detection (self-harm, suicidal ideation). Product is explicitly not framed as a mental-health app. No code path should ever imply otherwise.
- OUT (architectural constraint, not a product choice): per-entry edit/delete — entries are immutable; no `PATCH`/`DELETE /entries/:id` exists in the frozen backend. Real adoption-friction point for any future real-world use; cannot be changed within this project.
- OUT: offline writes — architecture is cloud-only; offline permits only viewing cached data, never creating entries.

## Technical context / constraints for downstream architecture work
- Flutter/BLoC/Clean Architecture, iOS portrait-only, frozen Supabase backend (23 endpoints via `x-cerne-function` naming, never literal REST paths).
- AI split (server-side only, app never calls a provider directly): Claude Sonnet 5 for chat, Claude Haiku 4.5 for vision/OCR/PII-scrub/summaries/insights/dashboard narrative, Voyage AI voyage-4 for embeddings.
- Privacy/compliance baked into architecture: on-device Whisper STT (raw audio never leaves device — only the transcribed text syncs to the cloud), zero AI-pipeline data retention (RNF03), row-level security (RNF04), LGPD hard-delete (RNF05).
- RNF06: domain layer must import neither `package:flutter` nor anything from `data/`. RNF07: domain-layer test coverage ≥80%. RNF09: 5 write endpoints × 3 failure types = 15 tested network-failure scenarios.
- Delivery order (confirmed from requirements.md section 12): F000 → RF03 → RF01 → RF02 → RF07 → RF06 → RF04 → RF10 → RF08 → RF05 → RF09.
- **Unresolved contradiction, needs a decision before F000 implementation:** `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/research/technical-flutter-package-selection-.../research.md` recommends `drift` (SQLite) for local cache; `_bmad-output/forge/f000-foundation-decisions/forged-idea.md` overrides it to `Hive`, reasoning all filtering/pagination is server-side so no relational engine is needed on-device. Fix: explicitly mark `drift` as superseded in the research artifact.
- Hardest unbuilt technical problems: RF07's history screen depends on three independently-changing streams (auth, sync-badge, entry data) while BLoCs may not import each other directly; RF08's proactive-insight trigger must fire exactly once per satisfied condition (5 messages OR 2 min inactivity) without double-firing or missing the window.

## Resource & timeline (open, not estimated)
No deadline date, hours-per-week budget, or buffer exists anywhere in `docs/input/` or `_bmad-output/`. This is a genuine open question for the user (course calendar / defense date), not something inferable from the input package. Feasibility of the delivery order against RNF07/RNF09's testing bars cannot be assessed until this is known.

## Rejected framings (press release stage)
- Headline candidate "Cerne Lets You Actually Talk to Your Own Diary — Privately, and It Remembers" — rejected as too long, stacking unproven claims ("actually," "privately") directly in the headline.
- Any "AI companion" / "AI friend" framing — rejected deliberately, to stay clear of the companion-chatbot category currently under regulatory/reputational pressure (Replika-class fines and lawsuits).
- Leading with the on-device-privacy angle instead of the memory angle — rejected as the headline hook because "AI forgets me / generic responses" tested as the louder, more universal pain point in research; privacy is used as a supporting proof point instead.

## Known gaps flagged during Customer/Internal FAQ (actionable items)
- **Fast-follow, low cost:** add a static crisis-resources disclaimer/link — requires no detection logic, doesn't contradict the non-clinical scope, closes an uncomfortable silent gap (no mental-health signposting at all today).
- **Accepted trade-off, not fixable within this project:** per-entry immutability (no edit/delete); cloud-only writes (no offline capture); no automatic entry categorization.
- **Process fix, cheap:** reconcile the drift-vs-Hive contradiction before F000 starts.
- **Documentation fix, not a code change:** the written defense must explicitly name the mechanism-vs-quality scope boundary (see "Honest, unresolved tension" above) rather than leaving it implicit.
- **Undecided, needs the user's explicit call:** whether Cerne is a one-time academic artifact or is meant to survive into a job-application portfolio — changes how much distribution/"Getting Started" planning matters going forward.

## Verdict summary
Forged in steel: the memory/RAG differentiator (research-validated against real competitor gaps), the precisely-qualified privacy architecture, the non-clinical positioning as a timing advantage, and the already-demonstrated resource discipline (three extension features concretely cut, on record). Needs more heat: timeline/deadline (completely unknown), post-defense fate of the project, two cheap unactioned fixes (drift/Hive, crisis disclaimer). Cracks in the foundation: the quality-of-AI-insight scope boundary must be stated explicitly in the defense or it reads as an unexamined gap rather than a deliberate one; entry immutability is a real adoption-friction point that should be named as a known limitation rather than silently discovered later.

Forged in steel: the memory/RAG differentiator (research-validated against real competitor gaps), the precisely-qualified privacy architecture, the non-clinical positioning as a timing advantage, and the already-demonstrated resource discipline (three extension features concretely cut, on record).
